notes.meaning: As soon as Solomon finished praying, God sent fire from heaven to burn up the offerings. A burnt offering was an animal sacrifice burned whole on the altar as a gift to God. The fire was God's clear sign that He accepted Solomon's prayer and the new temple, just as He had sent fire for Moses and Elijah. Matthew Henry notes that the fire fell on the sacrifice instead of the people. He sees in this a picture of Christ, who took God's judgment in our place.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critics think this fire story was added later. They point out that it is missing from the account in 1 Kings 8, and they suggest the writer joined two different reports together.

notes.meaning: God's glory filled the temple so fully that the priests could not go in. They were filled with awe at the fire and the thick cloud of God's presence. After a while their courage came back, and they went on with the offerings.

The people saw the fire and the glory come down on the temple. They bowed with their faces to the ground. That showed deep respect, and it showed they felt unworthy to stand before God. Yet they did not run away. They praised God for His goodness and His faithful love, which never ends. Matthew Henry says it was God's mercy that the sacrifice was burned and they were not.

Moved by God's sign of favor, the king and the people brought even more sacrifices. The animals were offered through the priests, who placed the blood and fat on the altar. The king led the way, and the people followed his example.

The huge number of animals was probably the total offered over the whole two weeks of feasting. The dedication was the act of setting the temple apart for God. It was mainly made up of bringing the ark of the covenant inside and offering these great sacrifices. Everyone took part, each in their own role.

Every group did its job. The priests served and blew trumpets, and the Levites (the temple helpers) played music and sang. They used the instruments David had made. David had written songs of praise and arranged for the Levites to sing them. The chorus "His loving devotion endures forever" may come from Psalm 136.

There were so many offerings that the bronze altar could not hold them all. So Solomon set apart the middle of the courtyard as extra space for burning them. Peace offerings were sacrifices shared in a meal of fellowship with God. Matthew Henry says that in a time of need, even the pavement could serve as an altar.
The feast here is the Feast of Tabernacles. It was a harvest festival held in the fall. People came from the far north to the southern border of the land, so the whole nation was there.

First came seven days to dedicate the altar, and then the seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles. The Day of Atonement fell in between. That was the yearly day of sorrow for sin and of being made right with God. On the closing day the people gathered to hear God's word. Matthew Henry reminds us never to resent the time we spend worshiping God.

After the last day of the feast, Solomon sent the people home full of joy for all God's goodness. 1 Kings 8:66 says the eighth day. Commentators explain that the people were free to leave then, but many stayed until the next day.

Solomon finished both the temple and his palace, and he carried out all he had planned. Matthew Henry says those who begin by serving God often do well in their own work too. He adds that Solomon's success came by God's grace.

The fire showed in public that God accepted the prayer. Now God also answered Solomon in private, appearing to him at night as He had once before. He promised to make the temple His chosen place for sacrifice and prayer.

God speaks of times when He might send drought, locusts, or disease to punish His people. Matthew Henry thinks the locusts may also stand for greedy enemy armies. God asks four things of His people. They must humble themselves, pray, seek His face (His favor), and truly turn from their sin. Then He promises to forgive them and heal their land. That means ending the plague, removing the pests, and sending rain again. Forgiveness comes first, and healing follows.
God promises to watch over the temple and listen to prayers made there. This is His direct answer to Solomon's request that God would hear His people when they prayed toward that place.

God says His Name will be at the temple forever. In other words, He will make Himself known there, and people may call on Him there. His eyes and heart, meaning His care and attention, will rest on that house.

God makes Solomon a promise with a condition. If Solomon lives faithfully like his father David, God will keep his family on the throne, as He promised David. A covenant is a binding promise. Adam Clarke notes that later kings did not keep the condition, so the throne was finally lost.

God warns that if the people turn to other gods, He will pull them out of the land like weeds pulled up by the roots. Even the temple would not protect them. God would reject it and make it a joke among the nations. The Geneva Notes say that when people misuse what God gave for His praise, He takes away His blessings.
The temple, once so grand, would become a ruin, and people passing by would be shocked. Adam Clarke notes that no nation was ever so greatly blessed, and none so greatly punished when it turned away.

The answer to "why?" would be plain: the people left the God who rescued them from Egypt, and they served other gods. Adam Clarke points out that Israel's strength had always come from God alone. When they left Him, even weak enemies could defeat them.
